title: Upstream vs. Downstream Intervention Visualizer
description: An animated version of the public health river metaphor. A cohort of 60 people walks a riverbank and some fall in (become ill). Students switch on an upstream housing policy, a midstream smoking cessation program, and expanded downstream hospital capacity, then compare people ill, people treated, and burden remaining across runs. Illustrative model, not real data.
creator: Introduction to Public Health Project
subject: public health
social determinants of health
upstream interventions
downstream interventions
river metaphor
prevention
learning_objective: Compare upstream, midstream, and downstream interventions by analyzing how each lever changes the number of people who become ill, are treated, and are left untreated.
chapter_title: Health Equity and Social Determinants of Health

learningObjectives: Classify an intervention as upstream, midstream, or downstream
Compare how each type of intervention changes illness, treatment, and untreated burden
Explain why upstream action lowers the load on downstream services

controls.label: Start / Pause / Resume / New Run
controls.description: Starts a run of 60 people, pauses it, or starts the next run. The simulation starts paused.

controls.label: Reset
controls.description: Clears the completed runs table and turns all levers off.

controls.label: Housing policy (U)
controls.description: Upstream lever. Lowers the share of people who fall in from 50% to 20%.

controls.label: Smoking cessation (M)
controls.description: Midstream lever. Pulls 40% of people in the water back to shore.

controls.label: Expand hospital (D)
controls.description: Downstream lever. Shortens the hospital's time per patient.

simulation.modelType: Deterministic agent flow (illustrative, not calibrated to real data)
assumptions: 50% fall in at baseline, 20% with the housing policy
40% of people in the water are rescued when the midstream lever is on
The hospital treats one person at a time; expanding it shortens service time
limitations: Rates are teaching parameters, not estimates of real program effects
Cost and cost-effectiveness are not modeled
The time lag before an upstream policy takes effect is not modeled

pedagogical.interactionPattern: Comparison tool with a completed-runs table
keyQuestions: Which lever is the only one that lowers the number of people who become ill?
Why does the hospital treat a larger share of ill people when the housing policy is on?
commonMisconceptions: More hospital capacity is the main way to improve population health
Upstream interventions are not health interventions
assessmentOpportunities: Classify a new intervention as upstream, midstream, or downstream
State one limitation of the river metaphor
